subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Chandrasekhar limit is best described as:
options: the minimum mass needed to begin hydrogen fusion
the maximum mass (about 1.4 solar masses) of a stable white dwarf
the maximum temperature of a main-sequence star
the radius of a neutron star
questions.explain: A white dwarf can be supported by electron degeneracy pressure only up to about 1.4 solar masses, the Chandrasekhar limit.

questions.q: On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, the axes are conventionally:
options: luminosity against temperature, with temperature decreasing to the right
questions.explain: The H–R diagram plots luminosity (or absolute magnitude) against temperature (or spectral class), with temperature decreasing from left to right.

questions.q: In the transit method of exoplanet detection, a planet is inferred from:
options: a steady increase in the star's temperature
the planet's own emitted radio waves
a periodic small dip in the star's brightness as the planet passes in front
a permanent red shift of the star
questions.explain: As an exoplanet crosses in front of its star, it blocks a little light, causing a regular dip in the measured brightness.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the evolution of a low-mass star like the Sun?
options: red giant → main sequence → nebula → white dwarf
nebula → red giant → main sequence → supernova
main sequence → neutron star → black hole
nebula → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf
questions.explain: A Sun-like star forms from a nebula, fuses on the main sequence, swells into a red giant, then sheds its layers leaving a white dwarf.

questions.q: The Schwarzschild radius Rs of a mass M is given by:
questions.explain: The Schwarzschild radius is Rs = 2GM/c², obtained by setting the escape velocity equal to c.

questions.q: Gravitational potential due to a point mass is given by V = −GM/r. The negative sign indicates that:
options: work must be done against attraction to reach infinity, where V = 0
questions.explain: Potential is zero at infinity and negative elsewhere because the field is attractive, so energy is needed to escape to infinity.

questions.q: The gradient of a gravitational potential against distance graph gives:
options: the field strength (with a sign change)
questions.explain: g = −dV/dr, so field strength is the negative gradient of the potential.

questions.q: In an astronomical refracting telescope in normal adjustment, what is the role of the objective lens?
options: To produce a magnified virtual image for the eye
To correct chromatic aberration in the eyepiece
To form a real image of a distant object at its focal point
To increase the field of view only
questions.explain: The objective forms a real, inverted image of the distant object at its focal point, which the eyepiece then magnifies.

questions.q: The quantum efficiency of a CCD refers to:
options: the fraction of incident photons that liberate a detectable electron
the number of pixels in the detector
the ratio of focal length to aperture
questions.explain: Quantum efficiency is the fraction of incident photons that produce a stored charge, and for CCDs it is far higher (~70–90%) than for the eye or film.

questions.q: Escape velocity from a planet's surface is given by:
questions.explain: Equating kinetic energy to the magnitude of potential energy gives v_esc = √(2GM/R).

questions.q: The total energy (kinetic + potential) of a satellite in a stable circular orbit is:
questions.explain: E = KE + PE = ½(GMm/r) − GMm/r = −GMm/2r, which is negative for a bound orbit.

questions.q: Gravitational field strength g at a distance r from a point mass M is given by:
questions.explain: g = F/m = GM/r², independent of the test mass m placed in the field.

questions.q: At the surface of the Earth (radius R, mass M), g equals:
questions.explain: g = GM/R² evaluated at the Earth's surface.

questions.q: Dark energy is the term used to explain which observation about the universe?
options: that all stars have the same mass
that light bends around the Sun
that the expansion of the universe is accelerating
questions.explain: Observations of distant Type Ia supernovae show the cosmic expansion is accelerating, attributed to dark energy.

questions.q: The parallax angle p of a star (in arcseconds) is related to its distance d (in parsecs) by:
questions.explain: By definition of the parsec, distance in parsecs equals the reciprocal of the parallax angle in arcseconds.

questions.q: For a refracting telescope in normal adjustment, the angular magnification is given by which expression?
questions.explain: Angular magnification M = fo/fe, the ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length.

questions.q: For a satellite in a stable circular orbit, the centripetal force is provided by:
options: the gravitational attraction of the planet
questions.explain: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so GMm/r² = mv²/r.

questions.q: The work done moving a mass along an equipotential surface is:
questions.explain: There is no change in potential along an equipotential, so no work is done.

questions.q: Newton's law of gravitation states that the force between two point masses is proportional to:
options: the product of the masses and inversely proportional to r
the sum of the masses and inversely proportional to r²
the sum of the masses and inversely proportional to r
the product of the masses and inversely proportional to r²
questions.explain: F = GMm/r², so the force is proportional to the product of the masses and follows an inverse-square law with separation.

questions.q: Dark matter was first inferred largely because:
options: stars in galaxies rotate faster than the visible mass alone can explain
galaxies emit too much visible light
questions.explain: Galaxy rotation curves stay flat at large radii, implying far more (non-luminous) mass than we can see.

questions.q: On the magnitude scale, a star of apparent magnitude +1 compared with one of apparent magnitude +6 is:
questions.explain: A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a brightness ratio of exactly 100, and smaller magnitudes are brighter.

questions.q: For a source moving away at speed v ≪ c, the red shift z is given by:
questions.explain: The non-relativistic Doppler red shift is z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c, where Δλ is the observed wavelength increase.

questions.q: A parsec is defined as the distance at which a star subtends a parallax angle of one arcsecond using a baseline of:
questions.explain: A parsec is the distance giving a parallax of 1 arcsecond when the baseline is 1 AU (the Earth–Sun distance).

questions.q: Stefan's law for the luminosity (power output) of a star of surface area A and temperature T is:
questions.explain: Stefan's law gives L = σ A T⁴, so luminosity rises with the fourth power of absolute temperature.

questions.q: Type Ia supernovae are valuable as standard candles in cosmology because they:
options: all have the same surface temperature
reach a known, consistent peak absolute magnitude
occur only in our own Galaxy
questions.explain: Type Ia supernovae have a reliably consistent peak luminosity, so their apparent brightness gives their distance.

questions.q: The field lines of a radial gravitational field around a point mass:
options: point radially inward toward the mass
questions.explain: Field lines point in the direction of the force on a test mass, which is radially inward toward the attracting mass.

questions.q: In the radial-velocity method of exoplanet detection, the planet is revealed by:
options: a periodic Doppler shift of the star's spectral lines as it wobbles
direct imaging of the planet's surface
a transit dimming of the star
questions.explain: The orbiting planet tugs the star, producing a periodic blue/red Doppler shift in the star's spectral lines.

questions.q: An estimate of the age of the universe can be obtained from the Hubble constant H₀ as approximately:
questions.explain: Assuming a constant expansion rate, the age of the universe is approximately the reciprocal of the Hubble constant, 1/H₀.

questions.q: As you move from the Earth's surface to infinity, the gravitational potential:
questions.explain: V = −GM/r increases (becomes less negative) toward zero as r increases to infinity.

questions.q: Equipotential surfaces in a gravitational field are:
questions.explain: Equipotentials are always perpendicular to field lines, so no work is done moving along them.
